analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student aid to colleges whose degrees don't qualify graduates for required licensing exams.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tie a college's access to federal student aid — including Pell Grants, federal loans, GI Bill benefits, and other veterans' and military education money — to whether its programs actually work. If a program prepares students for a job that requires a license (like nursing, teaching, or many trades), the school would lose federal aid eligibility unless graduates are fully qualified to sit for the licensing exam where they live, and the school arranges required clinical placements or internships. Schools would also have to certify their career training programs meet accreditation and licensure prerequisites, warn students in writing when they don't, and be legally authorized in every state where their online students live.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and veterans who pay for degree or certificate programs meant to lead to licensed jobs, especially those who borrow or use GI Bill benefits. The bill protects the biggest federal source of tuition money from flowing to programs that leave graduates unable to take the licensing exam in their state — the core promise of the 'Worthless Degrees' title. It also protects students in online programs from unknowingly earning a credential that doesn't count where they live.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and veterans in licensed-occupation programs

how_it_helps.text: A college would be ineligible for federal student aid for any program preparing students for a licensed occupation unless graduates can sit for the required exam and meet licensure prerequisites in their own state and in any state the school advertises to [S3].
Schools must provide timely placement for pre-licensure requirements like clinical placements, internships, or apprenticeships, which are a common bottleneck in licensed fields [S2].

Before enrolling a student in a career training program that fails a state's licensure prerequisites, the school must notify the student and get a signed, handwritten acknowledgement that the student wishes to enroll anyway [S3].

The protections reach across federal aid programs: Title IV student aid, Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act funds, adult education funds, veterans' benefits under title 38, and military tuition programs under title 10 [S3].

Schools offering online or correspondence courses must be legally authorized in each state where their enrolled students live, with states maintaining public complaint processes, though existing interstate reciprocity agreements would still count [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and career schools — above all for-profit colleges and online program providers — that would have to restructure programs, arrange clinical placements, obtain state authorizations, or lose access to federal aid money that makes up a large share of their tuition revenue. The bill's own certification and reporting requirements add compliance costs across the sector.
analysis.who_pays_short: Colleges, especially for-profit and online providers

drawbacks.text: The penalty is all-or-nothing: a school would lose aid eligibility for an entire licensed-occupation program rather than face a graduated sanction, which could push colleges — including needed nursing and allied-health programs — to simply stop offering them rather than fix them [S3].

Requiring state-by-state legal authorization for online programs adds a real compliance burden; the bill preserves interstate reciprocity agreements but lets any state in an agreement pile on extra requirements [S3].

The handwritten acknowledgement lets a school keep enrolling students into a program that fails a state's licensure prerequisites, as long as the student signs a statement that they want to proceed anyway — a warning, not a prohibition [S3].

The bill gives no additional funding to schools to expand clinical placements or internships, which are already scarce in fields like nursing, so schools may struggle to meet the placement requirement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students and taxpayers, the upside is large: it conditions federal tuition money on degrees that actually qualify graduates to work. For colleges, the cost is real but largely conditional — schools with sound programs keep their aid; schools whose graduates can't get licensed lose it. The main design weakness is the blunt all-or-nothing penalty and the loophole allowing students to sign away the protection. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the compliance costs, which is part of why the bill's total lack of cosponsors stands out.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and, after a subcommittee referral, never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on March 21, 2023, with no cosponsors [S1].
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs Committees [S5].
On April 11, 2023, it was referred to the Education and Labor subcommittee on Economic Opportunity; no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The bill had zero cosponsors and never reached a floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges and career schools that would have been exposed — particularly for-profit and online providers — kept the existing aid rules unchanged, and no student protections took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges whose programs would have faced aid cuts

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party and never came to a vote, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.note: These schools rely heavily on federal student aid for revenue and concentrate in licensed-occupation career programs; the bill would make programs ineligible for aid unless graduates can actually qualify for licensure exams, directly threatening tuition revenue built on degrees that don't lead to the advertised job.

The bill requires state-by-state legal authorization and complaint processes for online programs, adding compliance costs, but preserves existing interstate reciprocity agreements. Students in online programs currently have little recourse when a credential doesn't count in their home state.

The bill requires career programs to hold recognized accreditation and any federally or state-mandated programmatic accreditation, reinforcing accrediting agencies' gatekeeper role over which programs keep federal aid eligibility.
